name: Design a Webhook Delivery Platform
intent: Deliver millions of events to customers' own HTTP endpoints reliably, even when some of those endpoints are slow, flaky or gone, without letting one bad endpoint hurt anyone else.
codeTitle: signed deliveries with per-endpoint queues, backoff and a breaker
finalIntro: One invoice event reaching a customer's server, with a failure and a retry on the way.
prompt: Design the system that sends webhooks, like the ones Stripe or GitHub send. Customers register an endpoint URL and the event types they want. Internal services publish events. The platform must POST each event to every subscribed endpoint, retry failures for days, let receivers verify who sent a request and ignore repeats, show customers a log of every attempt with a way to replay events, and keep working when some customer servers are slow or down.
functional: Customers register, change and disable endpoint URLs, and choose the event types for each
Internal services publish events, and each event is delivered to every subscribed endpoint
Retry failed deliveries with a growing delay for up to three days
Sign every request so the receiver can verify it came from the platform and was not changed
Show a log of every delivery attempt, and let customers replay an event or a time range
Disable an endpoint that keeps failing, and tell the customer
Let customers rotate their signing secret without missing events
nonFunctional: Never lose an accepted event: it is durable before the publisher is told it was accepted
Deliver at least once, with a stable event id so receivers can drop repeats
A healthy endpoint gets its event within a few seconds of publication, even during a burst
One slow or dead endpoint cannot delay any other endpoint
Handle about 10,000 events per second at the peak, and one event may go to thousands of endpoints
Never let a customer's URL make the platform call its own internal network
Keep delivery logs for 30 days so that support and customers can see what happened

firstAttempt.text: When something happens, the service handling the request looks up the customer's URL and sends an HTTP POST to it before replying. If the call fails, it logs an error. There is no signature, no log of attempts, and the URL is called exactly as the customer typed it.
limits: A customer's slow server makes your own request wait, and a dead one makes it fail
A failed call is lost, because nothing remembers the event and nothing retries it
Anyone can send a fake request to the customer's URL, and the customer cannot tell the real one
A customer can register an internal address, and your server will call it for them
Customers cannot see what was sent or when, so every problem becomes a support ticket
An event with thousands of subscribers makes thousands of calls inside one request

steps.title: Write every event to a durable log first
steps.problem: Sending from inside the request that caused the event ties your own speed to the customer's server, and an event that fails to send is gone, because nothing recorded it.
steps.fix: The publisher appends the event to a durable, replicated event log and gets an answer as soon as the append is safe. If the event comes from a database change, it is written in the same transaction as that change, through an outbox, so an event exists exactly when the change does. Every event has a unique id, a type, a timestamp and a payload. A pool of delivery workers reads the log and sends the requests, so the publisher never waits for a customer.
steps.tradeoff: The publisher is fast and an accepted event can no longer be lost. There is now an extra hop and a log to run, and a delivery lags the event by at least the time the workers need to pick it up, normally well under a second.

steps.title: Fan out into one queue per endpoint
steps.problem: One event can have thousands of subscribed endpoints, and a single shared list of work mixes fast customers with slow ones, so a delay for one is a delay for all.
steps.fix: Fan-out workers read each event, look up the endpoints subscribed to its type in an index, and write one delivery job for each, into that endpoint's own queue. A job is the pair of event id and endpoint id, with a pointer to the stored payload rather than a copy. A very large fan-out is cut into chunks of subscriptions, handled by many workers in parallel, so one event with 5,000 subscribers does not hold up the next one. The delivery workers now read from the queues.
steps.tradeoff: Each endpoint has its own backlog, its own order and its own speed, and publishing is cheap whatever the number of subscribers. The number of jobs is events times subscribers, so the queue storage and the fan-out step must scale, and the subscription lookup must be fast.

steps.title: Give every endpoint its own limit, and stop calling a broken one
steps.problem: With one shared pool of workers, a customer whose server hangs for 10 seconds on every request ties up workers until none are left, and everybody's deliveries wait behind it. This is head-of-line blocking.
steps.fix: Each endpoint gets a concurrency limit, for example 3 requests in flight, a bulkhead that decides how many workers one customer can hold. Idle workers pick the next job from any endpoint that is below its limit, taking the endpoints in turn so none is starved. A short timeout, such as 10 seconds, bounds every call. A circuit breaker per endpoint opens after about 5 failures in a row: no calls are made for a while, jobs wait in the queue, and then one probe request tests the endpoint before the rest are released.
steps.tradeoff: A bad endpoint can cost at most its few workers, and healthy ones stay fast. A big and healthy customer may want a higher limit than the default, so limits need tuning, and a breaker that opens too easily delays events that would have been delivered.

steps.title: Retry with backoff and jitter over days, and give up gracefully
steps.problem: Customer servers go down for minutes or hours, and retrying at once, or on a fixed beat, either wastes workers on an endpoint that is still down or hits a recovering one with everything at the same moment.
steps.fix: A failed delivery goes to a retry timer and returns to its queue after a delay that grows, such as one minute, then 5, 30, 2 hours and so on up to a cap, for about three days, with a random amount of jitter so retries from many events do not line up. Every attempt is written to a delivery log with the time, status, latency and the start of the response. If an endpoint has failed every attempt for several days it is disabled, the customer is emailed, and events are kept so they can be replayed. The replay UI queues a fresh delivery for one event or a time range from the log.
steps.tradeoff: A short outage is healed without anyone noticing, a long one costs few resources, and customers can see and fix problems themselves. Events arrive late and out of order after an outage, and the logs of every attempt are a lot of data to store, which is why they expire after 30 days.

steps.title: Sign requests, number events, and say what order means
steps.problem: Anyone who learns the URL can post a fake event, someone on the network could replay a real one, and because delivery is at least once, the same event will sometimes arrive twice or out of order.
steps.fix: Each request carries a timestamp and a signature, an HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp and the exact body using a secret that only the platform and that endpoint share. The receiver recomputes it, compares in constant time, and rejects requests whose timestamp is more than about 5 minutes old. To rotate a secret, the platform signs with both the old and the new one for a day or two, and the receiver accepts either. Every request also carries the event id, which stays the same across retries, so receivers keep the ids they have handled and ignore repeats. The platform promises no global order. Events for one resource can be kept in order by sending them one at a time through one queue, and the payload carries a sequence or timestamp so the receiver can discard stale ones.
steps.tradeoff: Receivers can trust a request and safely ignore duplicates, and secrets can be changed with no downtime. Receivers have to write a little code, verifying the signature on the raw body bytes and storing ids. Strict per-resource order means one failing event holds back the later events for that resource, so most platforms keep it best-effort and recommend fetching the latest state.

steps.title: Call customers only through a locked-down egress proxy
steps.problem: The platform makes HTTP requests to addresses that strangers choose. A customer can register http://169.254.169.254/ or an internal admin service, or a name that points to a public address when checked and to an internal one when called, and the platform's own network becomes reachable (server-side request forgery).
steps.fix: All deliveries leave through an egress proxy in a network that cannot reach anything internal. The proxy accepts only https on allowed ports. It resolves the name itself, refuses loopback, private, link-local (including the cloud metadata address) and other reserved ranges, and then connects to the very address it checked, so the name cannot change in between. It does not follow redirects, or checks each hop again, and it limits response size and time. Registration also checks the URL and can send a test event.
steps.tradeoff: Customers cannot turn the sender against your network, and the rules live in one place that is easy to audit. Some customers have legitimate private or odd-port endpoints and need another path, such as a tunnel agent, and the proxy is one more piece that has to be fast and highly available.

failures.scenario: A customer's server is down for six hours
failures.impact: Their events cannot be delivered, and without care the retries would eat workers and the backlog would grow.
failures.answer: The breaker for that endpoint opens after a few failures and only occasional probes go out. Jobs wait in that endpoint's own queue, and nobody else is affected. When the server comes back, a probe succeeds, the breaker closes, and the backlog is delivered at the endpoint's concurrency limit, with jitter so it does not arrive as one burst.

failures.scenario: A customer's endpoint answers in 25 seconds
failures.impact: Each request holds a worker for a long time, so with a shared pool a few such customers would stop everyone.
failures.answer: The call is cut off at the timeout and counts as a failure, and the endpoint's own limit means it can hold only a few workers whatever its speed. Its breaker opens if the failures continue, and the customer's dashboard shows the latency. The advice to customers is to reply with a 2xx at once and do the work afterwards.

failures.scenario: The customer processed an event but our worker crashed before recording it
failures.impact: The platform thinks the delivery failed and sends the event again, so the customer sees it twice.
failures.answer: This is the price of at-least-once delivery, and it cannot be avoided without the customer's help. The retry carries the same event id, so the customer, who keeps the ids it has handled, ignores it. The platform's only duty is never to change the id and to document that duplicates happen.

failures.scenario: A customer's signing secret is leaked
failures.impact: Anyone with the secret can forge events that pass verification.
failures.answer: The customer starts a rotation in the dashboard: a new secret is created, and for the next day or two every request is signed with both. The customer deploys the new secret at their own pace, and then the old one is revoked. The timestamp check limits what a captured request can be used for, and the delivery log shows which events were sent in the meantime.

failures.scenario: A customer registers a URL that points at the cloud metadata service
failures.impact: Without checks, the platform would fetch its own instance credentials and might return them in the delivery log.
failures.answer: The egress proxy resolves the name and refuses private, loopback and link-local addresses before connecting, and it sits in a network with no route to the internal services anyway. Redirects are not followed, so a public URL cannot bounce to an internal one. Blocked attempts are logged and alerted on.

alternatives.title: Where the delivery jobs wait

options.name: One shared queue
options.pro: The simplest thing to build and run
options.con: One slow customer delays all the others, and the queue cannot separate them

options.name: A queue (or partition) per endpoint, with limits
options.pro: Isolation by design, and each customer has its own backlog and rate
options.con: Many small queues to manage, and a scheduler to pick fairly among them

options.name: A database table of jobs with a due time
options.pro: Easy to query, to show and to replay, and retries are just a new due time
options.con: Needs careful locking and indexing to reach tens of thousands of jobs per second

alternatives.pick: A job table or log holding every delivery, with a fair scheduler that keeps a per-endpoint limit. It is also what powers the delivery log and the replay UI.

alternatives.title: Ordering

options.name: No ordering promise
options.pro: Highest throughput, and a failed event blocks nothing
options.con: Receivers can see an update before the create it follows

options.name: Order per resource
options.pro: Events about one invoice or one repository arrive in sequence
options.con: A failure holds back that resource's later events, and it needs a key and a single in-flight request per key

options.name: Order for the whole endpoint
options.pro: The easiest model for the receiver
options.con: One failing event stops everything for the customer, and nothing can be sent in parallel

alternatives.pick: Best effort by default, with a sequence number or timestamp in each payload and advice to fetch current state. Offer per-resource ordering only for those who need it.

alternatives.title: How the retry delay grows

options.name: Fixed interval
options.con: A long outage costs a request every interval forever, and retries from one outage arrive in step

options.name: Exponential backoff
options.pro: Quick early retries for blips, and rare ones for long outages
options.con: Failures that began together still retry together

options.name: Exponential with jitter
options.pro: Retries are spread out, so a recovering endpoint sees a trickle instead of a stampede
options.con: The next try cannot be predicted exactly, which makes the dashboard less tidy

alternatives.pick: Exponential with jitter and a cap, for about three days.

alternatives.title: Push or pull

options.name: Push webhooks only
options.pro: The customer learns of an event at once
options.con: The customer must run a public server that can take the traffic

options.name: Pull from an events API
options.pro: The customer controls the pace, and has no public server to secure
options.con: Slower to notice, and constant polling wastes requests

options.name: Both: push, plus an events API for catching up
options.pro: Speed, and a way to recover anything that was missed

alternatives.pick: Push with an events API, so a customer who was down can read what they missed.
